extra.message: User-controlled parameter 'name' from the query string is directly interpolated into an HTML string (line 38) and then passed to Jinja2 Template().render() (line 41) without sanitization or autoescape. An attacker can inject malicious JavaScript via ?name=<script>alert(1)</script>.

Jinja2 Template() renders user-controlled content on line 41. The 'name' parameter (originally from query string ?name=) is embedded in the template string. An attacker can supply crafted template expressions like ?name={{ config }} or use Jinja2 object traversal to access sensitive attributes, read files, or achieve remote code execution.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code

extra.message: requests.get() at line 31 makes an outbound HTTP request to config.PUBLIC_IP_SERVICE_URL which is loaded from an environment variable. The URL scheme and destination are not validated or restricted. An attacker who influences this URL could cause server-side request forgery (SSRF), accessing internal services via file://, gopher://, or http:// protocols. Additionally, no timeout is set on the request — if the target service does not respond, the worker thread will hang indefinitely (CWE-400: Denial of Service). SSL certificate verification is also not explicitly configured.

The secret token SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN is hardcoded as a string literal ''5u93R53Cr3tT0k3n'' instead of being loaded from a secure secrets manager or environment variable at runtime (as the FIXME comment indicates). This value will be committed to version control and exposed in deployed artifacts.

The value SUPER_SECRET_NAME is hardcoded as ''John Ripper'' instead of being loaded from an environment variable at runtime (as the FIXME comment indicates). This reveals an internally secret name to any code path that reaches this endpoint.

The requests.get() call at line 31 has no timeout parameter. If the external IP service is slow to respond or unreachable, the worker thread will block indefinitely. In a concurrency-limited WSGI/ASGI server (like uvicorn), this can lead to resource exhaustion and denial of service for other users.

DEBUG mode is controlled via the DEBUG environment variable ('true', '1', 'yes', or 'y'). If set in production, FastAPI's debug mode exposes detailed error pages with stack traces and local variables to end users, leaking sensitive internal information.
